title: Detecting Perspective Shifts in Multi-Agent Systems
one_liner: When multiple AI agents evolving over time are locked in a black box, a new method spots the moment any of them shifts behavior.
lead: Picture running a thousand AI agents, each playing a different character or solving different problems. Weeks pass. One day something happens in the real world—a news event, a policy change, a system update. You wonder: did any of my agents actually change how they behave? This paper gives you the first practical way to know.

problem.h2: Why is it hard to notice when agents shift?
paras: Today, agent systems are black boxes. You send them a question and get an answer back, but you cannot see their inner workings. If you run the same agent every week for a year, its answers might slowly drift—different tone, different reasoning style, different priorities—but you would notice only if you read every single response by hand.

A naive approach: save one snapshot of the agent's behavior (a few sample questions and answers), then every week ask the same questions again and compare. But agents are random (they add randomness on purpose). The same question asked twice might yield slightly different answers just by chance. You cannot tell signal from noise.

Even if you asked a thousand test questions, you still face a choice: How different is different enough to say the agent changed? If you pick a loose threshold, you'll see false alarms on random fluctuation. If you pick a strict one, you'll miss real shifts.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Instead of comparing raw answers, map each agent into a geometric space where its location encodes its behavior, do this over time to see the trajectory, then use a rigorous statistical test to ask: is that trajectory consistent with random noise, or did the agent genuinely shift?

steps.text: Pick a diverse set of queries that probe different aspects of the agent's personality, reasoning, or domain knowledge.
Send the same questions to all agents at regular intervals (weekly, daily, etc.).

steps.b: Step 3: Embed responses into behavior space
steps.text: Use a similarity-based method to convert answer patterns into a coordinate for each agent at each time point.
Plot each agent's path through the space over time, seeing if and when it moves.
Ask: Is this motion consistent with random fluctuation, or is it statistically significant change? Declare shifts when the test rejects randomness.

object.h2: The one thing the paper changes
paras: Instead of looking at raw agent answers (text), the paper maps each agent to a point in a coordinate space based on the _pattern_ of its answers across a set of test queries. That geometric location is what moves over time.

hidden.name: Agent trajectory & variance
paras: The hidden quantity is how far each agent drifts from its starting position in the behavior space, and whether that drift is bigger than random jitter would predict. The paper calls this the agent's _trajectory_. Early snapshots place an agent at location A. Later snapshots place it at location B. The distance between A and B is the drift. But randomness also causes noise, so the paper measures: Is the drift large enough that random fluctuation would almost never cause it?

The paper estimates this using a kernel perspective space—a method that converts response patterns into coordinates—and then builds hypothesis tests that compare the observed drift against a null hypothesis of pure random noise.

heat.caption: Darker means larger drift from baseline. Highlights show agents and times when real change is detected.

reads.html: The paper watches agent behavior over weeks or months. If an agent's replies to test questions land in a very different region of behavior-space than before, something changed. The paper says whether that difference is real or just randomness.

TDKPS embeds agents at each time point via a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) perspective, then tests whether the measured distance exceeds a confidence interval computed under the null hypothesis (stochasticity only). Tests are provided at both agent-level and group-level aggregations.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the causal chain
paras: The core insight: agent behavior lives in a high-dimensional space — a cloud of numbers encoding how the agent responds to queries. Two things can happen: the agent drifts through that space (real change), or it bounces randomly inside a small region (randomness). Separating signal from noise requires a model of what randomness looks like.

The paper's move: use a similarity-based method to build a low-dimensional map where agents sit as points. Then measure how far each agent travels between time snapshots. The farther it travels, the stronger the evidence for change. By comparing the observed travel distance against what pure randomness would cause, the paper computes how likely it is that the shift is real.

Why this works: A kernel is a mathematical tool for measuring similarity between two things (in this case, two sets of agent answers). By using it to embed agents into a space, the paper gets a fair and data-driven way to measure behavior. By running a statistical hypothesis test (comparing to randomness), the paper avoids crying wolf at every tiny jitter.

stages.s: Test queries sent to all agents, weekly
Collect responses at times t=1, t=2, t=3, ...
Map response patterns to kernel coordinates
Compute distance traveled between consecutive time points
Compare observed distance to what noise alone would cause
Report if change is statistically significant

math.h2: The equation and a worked example
math.words: The test statistic measures the squared distance the agent travels in kernel space at each time step, then asks whether that total distance is more than expected under pure randomness.
symbols: cumulative squared drift up to time t
kernel embedding of agent responses at time s
the set of responses from agent at time s
squared distance in the kernel space

worked.title: Tiny numeric example
lines: Week 1: Agent answer set X1 maps to kernel point (2.0, 1.5).
Week 2: Agent answer set X2 maps to kernel point (2.1, 1.4). Distance = sqrt((2.1-2.0)^2 + (1.4-1.5)^2) = sqrt(0.01 + 0.01) = 0.14. Squared = 0.02.
Week 3: Agent answer set X3 maps to kernel point (3.2, 0.9). Distance = sqrt((3.2-2.1)^2 + (0.9-1.4)^2) = sqrt(1.21 + 0.25) = sqrt(1.46) = 1.21. Squared = 1.46.
Cumulative drift M_3 = 0.02 + 1.46 = 1.48. Under pure randomness, the expected cumulative drift might be 0.3. Since 1.48 >> 0.3, we reject randomness and declare that the agent changed.

math.note: The squared distances accumulate over time; a real behavioral shift pushes the agent far enough that the total drift outpaces what noise alone would cause.

charts.title: Naive (compare answers directly)
charts.note: Raw answer comparison drowns signal in noise and scales terribly.

charts.title: This paper (similarity space + hypothesis test)
charts.note: Coordinate space representation plus rigorous testing separates real shifts from randomness.

items.html: If your test queries probe only one aspect of agent behavior (e.g., only political opinions, or only creative writing), you miss shifts in other dimensions. The method assumes your test set is diverse enough to catch all kinds of behavioral change.

items.b: The similarity method is mismatched to the data.
items.html: Choosing the wrong similarity function (or wrong hyperparameters) can place agent responses so that similar behaviors land far apart in the coordinate space. This adds noise to the trajectory and reduces power to detect true shifts.

items.b: Real behavioral change is too gradual.
items.html: If an agent drifts extremely slowly over months, random variance might drown it out on weekly samples. Detecting slow creep requires either more frequent sampling or longer observation.

With a well-designed test suite, an appropriate kernel, and a chosen confidence level that balances false alarms and missed detections, the method reliably flags genuine behavioral shifts and ignores random noise.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Create a simple simulated multi-agent system: a few agents that answer the same 20 test questions every week for 12 weeks. Midway through (week 6), programmatically change one agent's behavior (e.g., shift its response pattern in a measurable direction; perhaps it becomes more conservative, or more creative). Run the paper's method on this data. The method should detect the shift in the changed agent with high confidence (a low p-value or high test statistic), and report no significant shift in the other agents.
demo.metric_eq: p_value for agent shift = P(observed drift | pure randomness). Low p (<0.05) = shift detected.
demo.closing: The test must show: detection of the real mid-stream behavioral change in one agent, while other agents register no change; and a clear separation of the test statistic between the agent that was modified and those that were not.
